claim: Integrated HIV-1 DNA was significantly associated with plasma viral load (p < 0.001; r2 = 0.64).

claim: HIV-1 DNA levels after 48 weeks of ART were significantly lower than those measured at baseline (p < 0.0001 for all comparisons).
source: As expected, HIV-1 DNA levels after 48 weeks of ART were significantly lower than those measured at baseline (p < 0.0001 for all comparisons; Students t test) by 0.63 log copies/million CD4 cells for Total, and 0.59 log copies/million CD4 cells for Integrated (Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical comparison using Student's t-test with p-value and quantified decrease.

claim: Total HIV-1 DNA decreased by 0.63 log copies/million CD4 cells after 48 weeks of ART.

claim: Integrated HIV-1 DNA decreased by 0.59 log copies/million CD4 cells after 48 weeks of ART.

claim: In multivariable Cox regression models with HIV-1 DNA and CD4 cell count at TI, Integrated HIV-1 DNA retained significance (HR 2.81 CI (1.05–7.55) p = 0.04).

evidence: Statistical comparison showing significant change.

claim: In individuals who subsequently restarted ART after the TI (n = 15), there was no significant difference between the HIV-1 reservoir size pre-TI and at least 6 months after re-starting ART (p = 0.58).
source: Of note, in an analysis of those individuals who subsequently restarted ART after the TI–and for whom we had samples (n = 15)–there was no significant difference between the HIV-1 reservoir size pre-TI and at least 6 months after re-starting ART (p = 0.58; paired students t test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that any increase in HIV-1 DNA on stopping ART may be reversible if therapy is re-commenced.
evidence: Statistical comparison using paired Student's t-test with p-value.

claim: Any increase in HIV-1 DNA on stopping ART may be reversible if therapy is re-commenced.

evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing no significant difference in reservoir size.

claim: Patients with high Total HIV-1 DNA levels were more likely to have a first detectable VL greater than 400 copies/ml, whereas those with lower HIV-1 DNA levels were more likely initially to rebound below 400 but above 50 copies/ml (p = 0.0074).
source: In this small post-hoc analysis (n = 45), we found that rebound varied according to the HIV-1 DNA level at the time of TI. Patients with high Total HIV-1 DNA levels were more likely to have a first detectable VL greater than 400 copies/ml, whereas those with lower HIV-1 DNA levels were more likely initially to rebound below 400 but above 50 copies/ml (p = 0.0074; Fisher's exact test) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Fisher's exact test showing statistical significance in a post-hoc analysis.

source: Since first described nearly two decades ago a persistent reservoir of HIV-1-infected cells remains the main reason that HIV-1 infection cannot be cured (Chun et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1997; Wong et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational literature.

claim: The vast majority of intracellular HIV-1 DNA is thought to be replication incompetent.
source: These assays are open to criticism as the vast majority of intracellular HIV-1 DNA is thought to be replication incompetent, and qPCR is not able to discriminate between replication competent and incompetent viral DNA genomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding.

claim: qPCR is not able to discriminate between replication competent and incompetent viral DNA genomes.
source: These assays are open to criticism as the vast majority of intracellular HIV-1 DNA is thought to be replication incompetent, and qPCR is not able to discriminate between replication competent and incompetent viral DNA genomes.
